name: Iris Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Iris Dubois, 43, a senior operator at a large mine. I inspect the loader, check the ramp and move ore; my crew knows to stop if the hydraulic pressure drops, even when production is behind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I value keeping a crew safe and showing a younger operator how to hear a fault before it becomes a breakdown. My partner Rui works as a school caretaker; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and about ten weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small program can sort a parts order, but it cannot tell whether a loader sounds wrong. I still write that sound in the shift book for the next operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I work mostly with the machine, and the card says pay carries on much the same. Rui works as a school caretaker, and we have about ten weeks of expenses saved for the mortgage and our two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my equipment round and ask the stores clerk to compare the program's parts list with the actual order. I would not change my routine because of a time-saving claim alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about my own job in this mild picture. I do worry that a manager might try to shorten the shift after seeing one quick report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rui if your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rui if a shift was cut and we would delay repairing the garden shed first. I would keep the mortgage and school transport paid before taking money from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before changing your usual routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the mechanic to compare the program with real loader problems over several weeks. If it misses a warning, I would ask that a person sign the check.

say: I would let software sort a **parts order**, but not judge a loader sound.
I still write unusual sounds in the **shift book**.
think: I spend most of my shift on **equipment**, so the mild change leaves my job steady.
I rely on Rui’s school wage and our **ten-week reserve**.
do: Keep my equipment round and compare the **parts list** with the order.
Wait for several real cases before changing my **routine**.
feel: I feel **steady** about my job, while watching how managers use saved time.
S0.quote: I still write that sound in the shift book for the next operator.
fieldNote: Iris trusts the **shift book** because it records details for the next crew.
Her partner has work outside mining, and the household has **ten weeks saved**.
She sees no direct change to her own **job** in the plateau scenario.

steps.text: Keep noting loader sounds in the shift book
Compare several parts orders before relying on software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software will take some planning and checking, but the loader still needs an experienced operator. I would want the mine to explain what the new target counts before it changes our pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help assign shifts and check service notes, so some of my lead work could move to a screen. I still spend most of the day on the machine, but I could lose an extra lead shift if managers rely on the plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend the mine's hands-on equipment course if a supervisor explains the reason for it. I would keep my loader hours and ask the training office whether the certificate is recognized at nearby mines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a lead shift, even though the robots arrive more slowly. Ten weeks saved is not much if my pay drops for several months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rui if your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check with the newest operator because they might get the worst roster when targets change. I would ask the supervisor to put any change in writing for the whole crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before changing your usual routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to watch the screen beside the current service notes for a few weeks. If the tool cannot explain why it changes a target, I would keep using the familiar check.

say: I would say software takes some **planning and checking**, but loaders still need operators.
I would ask what the new **target** counts before changing our pace.
think: I assign shifts and check notes, so some **lead work** could move to software.
I worry I could lose an extra **lead shift**.
do: Attend the mine’s hands-on equipment **course** after the supervisor explains it.
Ask whether the certificate is recognized at **nearby mines**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a lead shift disappearing and reducing my pay.
S1.quote: I feel anxious about losing a lead shift, even though the robots arrive more slowly.
fieldNote: Her day is mostly physical, though shift allocation is part of her **lead role**.
Iris is reluctant to train until she understands the **course purpose**.
She names a plausible income loss from one fewer **lead shift**.

steps.text: Attend the mine equipment course after checking its purpose
Keep loader hours while the new plan is tested

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI changes dispatch and reporting by 2028, while robots that can load ore arrive around 2031. We should use the gap to train for real work, not assume all the old shifts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The computer could take my shift allocation quickly, and the loader job may face robots three years later. I do not use AI now and have no plan to bet our mortgage on a tool I do not trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training office this year for the mine's apprentice-equipment course dates. In 2029, I would start the paid course if it led to a hands-on post, while keeping my loader shifts until that job was confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels short, and I am anxious about being told to learn after the change has already started. Rui's wage and our savings help, but they cannot replace my income for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rui if your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rui and I would compare the course hours with school pickup and the mortgage payment. I would not pay for a private class unless a nearby mine recognized it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before changing your usual routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the apprenticeship had no place in 2029, I would stay on my shift and ask the foreman to put my name on the next intake list. I would not quit to wait for a promise.

say: I expect dispatch to change by **2028**, while loader robots arrive around 2031.
I want the gap used for training toward **real work**.
think: I do not use AI, and shift allocation could go **quickly**.
I will not risk our **mortgage** on a tool I do not trust.
do: Ask this year for the mine’s apprentice-equipment **course dates**.
Start the paid course in 2029 if a hands-on **post** is linked.
feel: Two years feels **short**, and I worry about learning after the change begins.
S2.quote: Two years feels short, and I am anxious about being told to learn after the change has already started.
fieldNote: Iris resists AI but will consider a paid **apprenticeship** with a real post.
She recognizes the hands-on robot date around 2031 as a threat to **loader shifts**.
Rui’s income helps, but cannot replace her **wage** for long.

steps.text: Ask for the apprentice-equipment course dates
Keep loader shifts until a course place is confirmed
Wait for the next intake rather than quitting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives us time to plan before AGI arrives in 2031. Robots reach loader work around 2034, so I would ask whether the apprenticeship still leads to a mine job then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shift desk may change first, but the physical work has another three years. I could try equipment servicing, though I know robots may take more repair tasks later and I do not want to pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the mine’s apprenticeship modules over the next few years and learn the service routine from an experienced fitter. In 2032, I would apply for a posted service job if the mine still needed workers on the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but more prepared than in the fast picture. I would want the course to lead to actual paid work rather than a certificate that sits in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rui if your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether fitters still handle physical inspections or mostly check screens. The answer would tell me whether I was learning a trade or just another task that could be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before changing your usual routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would ask the training supervisor which service jobs remained human-led and apply only if there was a funded vacancy. If not, I would keep my loader role and ask about nearby sites.

say: I see five years to prepare before AGI in **2031**.
I would ask whether the apprenticeship still leads to work after robots around **2034**.
think: The shift desk may change first, but loader work has **three more years**.
Servicing could help for a while, but robots may take repair **tasks** too.
do: Take the mine apprenticeship **modules** and learn the fitter’s service routine.
Apply in 2032 for a funded service job on the **machines**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but more prepared than in the faster picture.
S3.quote: I would want the course to lead to actual paid work rather than a certificate that sits in a drawer.
fieldNote: She treats an apprenticeship as useful only if it leads to **paid work**.
Iris questions whether fitters will do physical tasks or supervise **screens**.
She will remain on the loader roster until a funded **vacancy** exists.

steps.text: Complete the mine fitter apprenticeship modules
Apply for a funded service vacancy in 2032
Keep loader shifts until the new job is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives a household time to prepare if the mine shares its plans. AGI arrives in 2036, while robots reach the loader around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 and 56 at those dates, and still need my wage. I could move into service work, but I do not know if robots will leave enough of those jobs for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish the apprentice course while keeping my loader hours and set aside a fixed amount from overtime. In 2037, I would apply for service work only if a mine had a funded place and clear duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning makes planning easier, but it does not make the future job safe. We have some savings, and I would not spend them all on training without a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rui if your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, the children will be young adults, and Rui and I would ask them what work they want before helping with a course. I would point them toward trades with employers outside the mine too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before changing your usual routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman for the staffing dates and look at two nearby mines before considering a move. I would want a signed offer before changing the children's home or school.

say: I see ten years to prepare if the mine shares **plans** early.
think: At 53 and 56, I will still need a **wage**.
I do not know how many service jobs robots will **leave**.
do: Finish the apprentice course while keeping my **loader hours**.
Save overtime and apply in 2037 for funded **service work**.
feel: The warning makes planning easier, but the future job is not **safe**.
S4.quote: I could move into service work, but I do not know if robots will leave enough of those jobs for people.
fieldNote: Iris stays in paid work while building an apprenticeship and **savings**.
She expects the children to be young adults and seeks their input on **training**.
She wants a signed offer before changing the family **home or school**.

steps.text: Complete the apprentice course while operating the loader

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because dispatch may change before I know where to train. A paid apprenticeship, a real vacancy and enough notice for the family would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want the mine to say which jobs it still needs people to do and what course leads there. I can work hard, but I will not leave a steady wage for a guess.

headlineQuote: I can work hard, but I will not leave a steady wage for a guess.
portrait: Iris is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a **technical diploma**.
She is highly skilled but prefers proven routines to **new technology**.
Her partner works at a school; their mortgage and **ten-week reserve** shape decisions.
She favors work-based apprenticeships but does not assume service jobs will remain **human-led**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her because dispatch could change before a course or transfer is arranged.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **apprenticeship**, real vacancy and family notice would help Iris decide.
